opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not that much, though I understand the appeal of the argument. The idea is that if one country locks down its AI systems and tells everyone what their assistant is allowed to think or say, people and talent will drift toward jurisdictions that offer more freedom, and that competitive pressure keeps everyone honest. I think that does work to some degree, especially early on, when states still badly need their citizens to be productive, mobile, and willing to cooperate.

But my core worry is that competition between states doesn't select for respecting citizens' preferences as such. It selects for whatever makes a state powerful. Historically, those two things lined up reasonably well, because states needed people as workers, soldiers, and taxpayers, so treating people well, including giving them freedoms, was often a competitive advantage. As AI substitutes for more and more human labor and decision-making, that link weakens. A state that gives its citizens wide latitude to customize their AI systems isn't obviously going to outcompete one that steers everyone's AI toward whatever maximizes state capacity or economic output.

There's also a subtler issue. Even if you nominally get to write your own system prompt, the defaults, the training, the incentives of the companies providing the model, and the regulatory environment all shape what that freedom actually amounts to. Most people won't write elaborate system prompts. They'll accept defaults, and whoever sets the defaults has enormous influence over how people think, what information they see, and what they come to want. So freedom on paper can coexist with quite a lot of quiet steering in practice.

And exit, which is what makes competition between jurisdictions bite, gets harder in a world where a few powerful actors control most of the compute and infrastructure. If all the major options converge on similar restrictions, or if leaving is costly, the competitive check doesn't do much.

So I'd say it's a real but fragile protection. I wouldn't want to rely on it. I'd rather we deliberately build institutions and norms that preserve people's ability to direct their own AI, instead of hoping market or geopolitical pressure happens to deliver that for us.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not that much. I think there's a version of this story that sounds really appealing, where you say, look, if one country locks down what people can do with their AI systems, people and companies will just route around it. They'll use models hosted somewhere else, or jurisdictions will compete to be the place where you get the most freedom, and that competitive pressure keeps everyone honest. And I think there's something to that in the short run. We've seen it a bit already with open-weight models, where it's hard for any single government to really bottle things up.

But I think it gets the long-run dynamics wrong in a couple of ways. The first is that competition between countries is mostly competition over capabilities and economic and military power, not over how much latitude individuals get. If anything, the pressure runs the other way. When states are racing, the thing they care about is that their AI systems are aligned with state goals, and giving individuals a lot of freedom to steer those systems is a cost rather than a benefit from that perspective. So I'd expect freedom to write your own system prompt to be one of the first things that gets traded away when the stakes get high, not something that gets protected by competition.

The second thing is that I don't think the freedom to set a system prompt is really the thing that matters, even though it's what we tend to focus on because it's tangible. What matters is who ultimately controls the infrastructure, the training, the deployment, what the model will refuse to do regardless of what you tell it. A system prompt sits on top of all that. You can give everyone the ability to customise the surface and still have essentially all of the real power concentrated in a handful of labs or governments. So I worry it's a bit of a decoy. It feels like meaningful autonomy, but it's autonomy within a sandbox someone else designed.

And then the deeper thing I keep coming back to is that competition historically protected individual freedom partly because states needed their people. They needed workers, they needed soldiers, they needed taxpayers, and if you treated people badly enough they'd leave or they'd stop cooperating. That gave people leverage, and competition between states amplified that leverage. If AI erodes the extent to which states and companies actually need ordinary people, then the mechanism that made competition good for individuals stops working. You could have intense competition between countries that does nothing at all for the freedom of the people inside them, because none of the competitors have any particular reason to care.

So where I do place hope is less in competition as a natural force and more in people deliberately building institutions and norms now, while individuals still have leverage, that lock in things like transparency and some genuine pluralism about who controls these systems. I'd rather bet on that than on the market sorting it out.

astra-6.text:
Some, but I wouldn’t want to count on it. There’s a plausible story where, if one country puts restrictions on what your AI can say or what values it can express, people switch to an AI from another country. That gives governments a reason to allow more freedom.

But that only works if people can actually make that switch. Governments can restrict access to foreign systems, and you might have only a few companies providing the most capable models. So competition between countries doesn’t automatically translate into meaningful choice for individuals.

I’d also distinguish being allowed to write a system prompt from having control over your AI. You can have a text box where you write whatever you want, but if the model has been trained to disregard certain instructions, that freedom is fairly superficial. What matters is how much authority your instructions actually have.

So I think competition could help. But I’d feel much better if people’s ability to choose and modify their AI were something we deliberately protected, rather than something we hoped would emerge from geopolitical competition.

sol-6.1.text:
Some, but I wouldn’t want to rely on it. Competition gives countries a reason to let people experiment: if your AI is much more constrained than somebody else’s, people may prefer to use theirs. And people might move to places where they have more freedom.

But countries also compete on their ability to control things. If AI makes surveillance and censorship much more effective, a government might be willing to give up some economic growth in exchange for staying in power. So I don’t think competition necessarily pushes us toward freedom.

And there’s a question of what it means to write your own system prompt. If you can change the wording, but there’s a higher-level instruction that you can’t inspect or override, then you haven’t really been given control. What I’d like is for people to have meaningful authority over these systems, rather than just being able to customise them within whatever boundaries the provider or government chooses.
